[[SOURCE-CODE]] [[LINE01]] #Step 1: Define the function [[LINE02]] def concat_chars(a, b): [[LINE03]] new_a = b[:2] + a[2:] [[LINE04]] new_b = a[:2] + b[2:] [[LINE05]] return (new_a + " " + new_b) [[LINE06]] #Step 2: Call the function [[LINE07]] print(concat_chars("Hello", "There")) [[LINE-EXPLANATIONS]] [[LINE02.EXPL1]] We need to first declare the function so that we can call it later. The following lines declare the function concat_chars that receives two strings and returns a string formed from the given strings separated by a space character such that the first two characters of the given strings are swapped. The 1st string is referred by variable a and the 2nd string is referred by variable b.

Note that all statements following the header line are indented. [[LINE03.EXPL1]] This statements sets variable new_a to the string that is formed from the first two characters of the 2nd string followed by the 1st string without its first two characters.

b[:2] fetches the first two characters of the 2nd string.
a[2:] fetches all characters beyond the second character in the 1st string. [[LINE03.EXPL2]] Note that we can get ranges of characters in a string by slicing, that is by providing a pair of offsets separated by a colon in square brackets after the string (e.g., s[1:3]). The left offset is taken to be the lower bound (inclusive), and the right is the upper bound (non-inclusive). That is, Python fetches all characters from the lower bound up to but not including the upper bound. If omitted, the left bound defaults to 0 and the right bound defaults to the length of the string that we are slicing. [[LINE04.EXPL1]] This statements sets variable new_b to the string that is formed from the first two characters of the 1st string followed by the 2nd string without its first two characters.

a[:2] fetches the first two characters of the 1st string.
b[2:] fetches all characters beyond the second character in the 2nd string. [[LINE04.EXPL2]] Note that we can get ranges of characters in a string by slicing, that is by providing a pair of offsets separated by a colon in square brackets after the string (e.g., s[1:3]). The left offset is taken to be the lower bound (inclusive), and the right is the upper bound (non-inclusive). That is, Python fetches all characters from the lower bound up to but not including the upper bound. If omitted, the left bound defaults to 0 and the right bound defaults to the length of the string that we are slicing. [[LINE05.EXPL1]] This statement returns the result of the concatenation of the string values stored in variables new_a and new_b sepeated by a space character. [[LINE05.EXPL2]] The return statement, when reached, ends the function call and sends the result back to the caller. [[LINE07.EXPL1]] This statement prints to the default standard output stream the string returned from the function call. Note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned string from the function call in a variable. We could use the string returned from the function call directly in the print function. [[LINE07.EXPL2]] Note that the function call must be done after the function is declared. [[LINE-DISTRACTORS]] [[DIST1.LC]] new_a = a[:2] + b[2:] [[DIST2.LC]] new_b = b[:2] + a[2:] [[DIST3.LC]] new_b = a[2:] + b[:2] [[DIST4.LC]] new_a = b[2:] + a[:2] [[TASK-INSTRUCTIONS]] Translate the given worked example into Arabic. Be sure to specifically translate the sections labeled [[PROGRAM-NAME]], [[PROGRAM-DESCRIPTION]], [[SOURCE-CODE]], [[LINE-EXPLANATIONS]], and [[LINE-DISTRACTORS]]. In the [[SOURCE-CODE]] section, translate ONLY user-defined string-literals and comments; make sure they are ASCII-folded (i.e., remove any accents or non-ASCII characters). Preserve the original format and Do NOT add, remove, or change any content beyond translation.
